title: 'He didn't know Willie Pickton at all'
article: Steve Remian was "disgusted" to learn his name was linked to the trial of accused serial killer Robert (Willie) Pickton, a longtime friend says.
Remian was shot dead by Halton police early Saturday after he confronted officers who had trailed him to a park in Oakville.

Earlier this year, Remian was briefly in the spotlight at Pickton's trial when it was revealed a suitcase belonging to him was found at Pickton's farm. Police also found Remian's hair on a blanket spattered with the blood of a woman Pickton is charged with killing.
The RCMP in B.C. said yesterday it was aware of Remian, but did not consider him a suspect in the case.

"Steve Remian was known to the Missing Women Task Force," the RCMP announced in a statement. "However, he was not a suspect nor was he a person of interest in relation ... any of their investigation."

Alex Hunter of Victoria, who befriended Remian a dozen years ago, told the Star the suitcase and hair arrived at Pickton's farm in the trunk of another friend's car, which was sold to Pickton for scrap after the friend died in 2000.
"He didn't know Willie Pickton at all," Hunter explained. "He was disgusted. He phoned me in a panic."

Remian had gone wandering around British Columbia and had left some belongings at the friend's home when the man was killed in a dock accident in Burnaby, he said. Hunter said he reclaimed Remian's briefcase, but didn't know about the other possessions.
"Steve would take off and travel for months or years at a time," Hunter recalled. "His life was in a shambles.
"It was a struggle for him just to exist. He had trouble fitting in with society. He was desperately seeking love and acceptance from people.
"He walked around with a huge massive hole in his heart and he constantly tried to fill that hole."
Hunter said Remian, who had three children under 13 from whom he was estranged, had struggled with issues from his own childhood to which he never found answers.
"He'd be in relationships or in a job or something and his head was full of bad wiring because of these things that were unresolved. He'd just react by getting up and going away."

He said Remian returned to Ontario earlier this year after losing a job at a diamond mine in B.C. Remian had lined up a job at a Sudbury mine, but blew that off when he began a relationship with a woman in Oakville.
"He said he needed a woman in his life, someone he could come home to," Hunter said.
It was in Oakville's Wedgewood Park, beside the elementary school he attended as a child, that Remian died in a hail of police bullets early Saturday.
Police followed him there after receiving a report of a man with a rifle outside a Tim Hortons coffee shop on Trafalgar Road.
Witnesses at the coffee shop said the man had threatened to harm himself and others.

Shortly after 2:30 a.m., three officers shot at Remian as he emerged from a late-model four-door Cadillac with B.C. licence plates. Hunter, who last heard from Remian by e-mail two days before his death, said he wasn't surprised by such speculation.
"He was struggling with demons and he just didn't want to go on," he said. "He was in an ugly world and didn't have the tools to survive."
